paragraphs.heading: A core brighter than its stars
paragraphs.text: An active galactic nucleus, or AGN, is a compact region at the heart of a galaxy that gives off a large amount of energy which does not come from its stars. That energy has been detected in radio waves and microwaves, in infrared, visible and ultraviolet light, and in X-rays and gamma rays. AGN are small yet stay extremely bright over long periods. They are the most luminous lasting sources of radiation in the universe, so astronomers can use them to find distant objects.

paragraphs.heading: Fed by a black hole
paragraphs.text: The radiation is thought to come from accretion, the gathering of matter by a supermassive black hole sitting in the middle of the host galaxy. In 1964 Edwin Salpeter and Yakov Zeldovich suggested this as the power source of quasars. From the late 1960s on, astronomers have argued that an AGN needs to be driven by black holes of 10⁶ to 10¹⁰ times the Sun's mass. Accretion can turn energy of position and motion into radiation very efficiently, which helps explain the steady, high brightness that is seen.

paragraphs.heading: The accretion disc
paragraphs.text: In the standard model, cold material close to the black hole forms an accretion disc. Processes in the disc move matter inward and angular momentum outward, and they heat the disc up. The disc's light is expected to peak in the optical and ultraviolet range. Above it, a corona of hot material can scatter some photons up to X-ray energies. The disc's radiation also excites cold atoms near the black hole, which then glow at particular emission lines.

paragraphs.heading: Dust and jets
paragraphs.text: Gas and dust near the disc may hide a large share of the radiation, but in a steady state that energy is given off again at another wavelength, most likely infrared. Some discs also produce twin jets, narrow and fast outflows that shoot out in opposite directions from near the disc. Each jet points along either the disc's angular momentum axis or the black hole's spin axis. Early X-ray observations in the 1960s and 1970s showed that Seyfert galaxies and quasars shine strongly in X-rays, light that comes from the inner parts of these discs.

paragraphs.heading: Many faces, one engine
paragraphs.text: What an AGN looks like depends on the black hole's mass, how fast it is fed, the orientation of the disc, how much dust blocks the view and whether jets exist. Many subclasses have been named from these observed traits, and the most powerful are called quasars. A blazar is an AGN whose jet points toward Earth, its light boosted by relativistic beaming. Since supermassive black holes seem to sit in most if not all massive galaxies, AGN-like behavior is expected whenever a supply of material comes within a central black hole's reach.

paragraphs.heading: From mystery to model
paragraphs.text: Viktor Ambartsumian introduced the idea of active galactic nuclei in the early 1950s. At the 1958 Solvay Conference he argued that explosions in galactic cores throw out large amounts of mass, and that such cores must contain bodies of huge mass and unknown nature. His idea was met with skepticism at first. A major step came in 1963, when Maarten Schmidt published a measurement of the redshift of the quasar 3C 273. Today AGN are a major topic of research, both in observation and in theory.
